quota_value_note: quota_value is list-price USD of usage per USD of subscription capacity consumed. It comes only from a dated astrocyte measurement or a figure the operator states, never an estimate made here. Absence is unknown, not zero; not_established records why nobody has established a figure. Measured values are reviewed after 30 days.
unit_policy: US list price, monthly-billed, web subscription. An operator on an annual term, in another country, or subscribed through an app store pays something else, and this plane cannot see which.
how_to_add_a_row: Open the source_ref, read the number, and record what the page says. If the page does not publish the number for that tier, the row is a refusal with why — never the figure you remember. The establisher is whoever looked, and the date is when they looked, both from the first row rather than retrofitted. WHEN A REFUSAL BECOMES A PRICE, KEEP WHAT THE REFUSAL RULED OUT. A refusal cell does two jobs that age differently: 'we could not source this', which goes stale the moment the row lands, and 'here is what sourcing it cost and which surfaces did not have it', which never does. Replacing the note with a bare price discards the second, and the next reader who wonders why the row is not sourced from the vendor re-runs every search that produced it. The store keeps both eras by construction; this file is what a human reads, so the ruled-out record has to be carried forward by hand.
review_interval_note: review_by is a ceiling on how long a wrong value may circulate, NOT a sampling rate. Nothing reveals a plan reprice: every other fact in this store has a fetch that would eventually contradict a stale value, and this one has the review and nothing else. The damage is retroactive, because every window in the stale period was priced against the wrong number. Quarterly, and the derivation travels with the number because the first person to find the review tedious will reason from frequency and be right about the frequency.

quota_value.basis: List-price value of in-scope tokens divided by (weekly-window quota points used x fee per point), fee per point = monthly price x 7/30 / 100. Pooled across 5 accounts. Daily rows 2026-10-01..10-09, each covering the trailing 7 days. Excludes the 09-25/26 rows (85-88x), recorded before the series settled. Reads 1-2% high, because usage between the last reading and a reset is lost.
quota_value.token_mix: Agentic coding, 98.5% cache read, 1.3% cache write, 0.13% output, 0.07% reasoning, 0.01% input, over 44.9B tokens. A chat-heavy mix would read differently.

cells.note: Kept as a row rather than dropped because a consumer holding an API string queries THIS key, and an absent key answers with no_coverage — which sends a reader looking for a curation gap that does not exist. A refusal that POINTS costs one line and saves a search.

why_this_basis: US list price, MONTHLY-BILLED basis. Recorded rather than assumed, and the basis is chosen for its FAILURE DIRECTION rather than for consistency: a higher denominator produces a lower multiplier, so recording the monthly-billed price makes a subscription look WORSE than it is for an annual subscriber. Every other known residual in the consuming calculation biases toward 'keep paying', so the one term that errs pessimistic is the one pushing back. Do not 'correct' this to the annual figure: it would remove the only conservative term. anthropic/pro is $17 billed annually against $20 monthly, a 15% spread, and that difference is deliberately not modelled here — an operator on an annual term or a grandfathered rate overrides this plane on their own credential record, which is where a fact about one account belongs. WEB-SUBSCRIPTION prices, additionally: the Max help centre states 'these prices are for web subscriptions only. Mobile pricing may vary depending on your app platform.' An operator who subscribed through an app store may pay an app-store markup this plane cannot see, which is a third basis axis beyond country and billing term. Same remedy as the others — the credential override carries what one account actually pays.
tier_vocabulary: The tier is the VENDOR'S OWN TIER NAME, never an API plan string. OpenAI's Pro 100, Pro 200 and Pro 500 are pro_100, pro_200 and pro_500 here. A consumer holding an API string must map it to a tier itself, with knowledge of the account.
why_tier_vocabulary: The tier column is the VENDOR'S OWN TIER NAME, never an API plan string. OpenAI now publishes Pro 100, Pro 200 and Pro 500; Pro 5x/pro_5x and Pro 20x/pro_20x were the earlier names. A consumer holding an API string must map it to a tier name itself, with knowledge of the account — the same shape as mapping a quota source's provider naming onto models.dev slugs. Keying this plane on API strings would make one source_ref cover two claims of different strength: the page establishes what a tier costs, and nothing published establishes which tier an API string names. The renamed keys are not aliases: removing the old rows makes the file-diff mechanism tombstone them.
when_a_row_should_exist: COVERAGE HERE IS DEMAND-DRIVEN, NOT COMPLETENESS-DRIVEN. This catalog carries 12+ subscription planes (alibaba-coding-plan, kimi-code-plan-global, minimax-coding-plan and the rest) and this file prices two providers. That gap is correct until someone names a plane they hold. EVERY ROW COSTS A REVIEW, and the review date is this plane's only liveness signal — so rows nobody reads do not merely sit idle, they dilute the gate. A reviewer facing twelve overdue rows for planes no one subscribes to learns to clear them in a batch, and the one row that mattered clears with them. Minting a row for an unheld plane also asserts more than it looks: that the figure was sourced, is current, and will be re-checked. Absence asserts nothing and costs nothing. So the trigger is a named consumer with a named plane, not a sweep of what exists upstream.
